title: Tetzaveh: names over the heart (Exodus 28:12, 29)
hook: the high priest carries the tribes' names on his shoulders and over his heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, kohen, the priest, and garments for splendor and for beauty. Your line was clothes carry meaning. What did you wear on purpose? Today, still in Tetzaveh, what's written on those clothes. Day three hundred sixty-one.

Some people keep a list. Not a to-do list. A list of names. A grandmother who prays every night through her grandchildren, one by one, oldest to youngest. A nurse who keeps the first names of patients she's lost on a folded card in her wallet. A soldier with a buddy's name on a bracelet. We carry people this way, on paper, on metal, in our heads. The high priest of Israel was asked to carry an entire people this way, on his clothes, every time he went into the sanctuary. Twice over. In two different places on his body.
screen: `A LIST OF NAMES.` → `ON PAPER, ON METAL.` → `A WHOLE PEOPLE, ON HIS CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: First, the shoulders. On the ephod, the high priest's apron, there are two shoulder straps, and on each one sits an onyx stone. Engraved on the two stones, six and six, are the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, in the order they were born. The verse says Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial. Then, the heart. Hanging in front of his chest is the breastplate, the choshen: a square of woven cloth set with twelve precious stones in four rows of three. Each stone is engraved with one tribe's name. And here's the verse, in the old Jewish translation: "And Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart." Notice: the same twelve names, carried in two places. Some readers have dwelt on the difference. The shoulders are where you carry weight: a burden, a responsibility, the people as a load to bear. The heart is where you carry love: the people as people you care about. A leader needs both. Only shoulders, and the people become a weight. Only heart, and nothing gets carried. And notice one more thing. On the shoulders, two big stones hold six names each. On the heart, every tribe gets its own stone. On the heart, nobody is grouped. Each name is held one by one. Every time Aaron went in before God, he walked in wearing them all.
screen: `TWO ONYX STONES, SIX AND SIX.` · `THE CHOSHEN: TWELVE STONES.` · `SHOULDERS FOR WEIGHT, HEART FOR LOVE.` · `ON THE HEART, ONE BY ONE.` · then, large: `NAMES ON THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry some names. Settle, and breathe. Let a few names come to mind, people who need carrying right now. Someone sick. Someone grieving. Someone far away. Someone just starting something hard. Say each name slowly, one at a time, on its own. Don't group them. If you pray, you can hold each name before God, the way Aaron carried them. If you don't pray, simply let each name rest, for a breath, over your heart. The bell holds the time.
Tetzaveh. You shall command. Our portion, where the high priest carries the twelve tribes' names on his shoulders and over his heart.
Your line: names on the heart. Today, carry one person's name with you, and say it once, quietly, in prayer or in thought, by name. Day three hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Jews pray for the sick by name, often in the Mi Sheberakh prayer said during the Torah reading, where people call out the names of those who need healing, and in the Amidah's blessing for healing.

original.note: Hebrew: the breastplate of the high priest, set with twelve stones.

trapdoor: what you thought: decorative gems on a robe.
what it means: the people carried twice: as a weight on the shoulders and, one by one, over the heart.
what a scholar hears: 28:10 sets the shoulder names in birth order; 28:21 gives each tribe its own breastplate stone.
